text.p: These are the leading stories in the Namibian press on Friday.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Consensus was growing on Thursday that the president's ban on public demonstrations without the written approval of the Namibian police was unconstitutional and could be successfully challenged in court.

- One of eight accused in the Katutura Single Quarters Scam, in which the government was defrauded of five million Namibian dollars, was re-arrested after failing to register his house as guarantee for his N$100,000 bail granted over a fortnight ago.
- From 1998 the government will no longer grant hunting concessions. This function is to be taken over by conservancies in communal areas.

- The opposition DTA of Namibia has expressed shock over the decree by President Sam Nujoma that no public demonstrations will in future be allowed without the written approval of the police, saying it was ironic that the president had made use of the same tactics against which the national liberation forces had fought against.

- The two partners of the Swakopmund Hotel and Entertainment Centre, Transnamib and Stocks and Stocks are involved in a serious dispute centred around continued losses, which by the end of June amounted to about N$25 million. Transnamib's decision to withdraw from the loss-making enterprise has drawn threats of a court case from Stocks and Stocks.
- Justice minister Ngarikutuke Tjiriange has announced that a bill aimed at addressing rape and other violent crimes against women and children will be tabled in parliament soon.
